chunks: I asked him about the slave jointly owned between partners, when one of them emancipates his share. So he said: This is a spoiling/harm against his companions; he [the slave] is appraised at a price, and the one who emancipated him is liable for the price, because he has spoiled it against his companions.

key_terms.شُرَكَاء: partners/co-owners (shuraka) — multiple people who jointly own something
key_terms.فَسَاد: harm/spoiling (fasad) — causing corruption or damage to another's property rights
key_terms.مَمْلُوك: slave/owned person (mamluk) — one who is legally owned
key_terms.نَصِيب: share/portion (nasib) — one's allocated portion of a jointly-owned thing
key_terms.يَضْمَن: to be liable/guarantee (yadman) — to bear financial responsibility for damages
key_terms.يُقَوَّم: to be appraised (yuqawwam) — to have one's market value assessed

ai.seo_question: What happens in Islamic law if one co-owner emancipates a jointly-owned slave?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a legal ruling from one of the Imams (peace be upon him) regarding the emancipation of a jointly-owned slave by one co-owner. The Imam rules that such a unilateral act constitutes harm (fasad) to the other co-owners, and the emancipator must compensate them at full appraised value. This reflects the classical Islamic legal principle that one co-owner cannot unilaterally diminish the property rights of others, and that emancipation — while meritorious — must be done lawfully without infringing on others' rights.
